notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 60, drawn from the sources I was able to retrieve.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

**Traditional Protestant overview:** Most older commentators (Gill, Barnes, Henry) see this chapter as a prophecy of the Gospel age — the ingathering of Gentiles into the Church under the Messiah. It is read in many traditions as the Epiphany lesson. The imagery of light breaking into darkness, nations streaming to Zion bearing gifts, and the transformation of the city is understood as the Church glorified by Christ.

**Dispensational / Premillennial view (Guzik, Constable):** The chapter is directed specifically to ethnic Israel and awaits literal fulfillment in the Millennial Kingdom when Jesus reigns from Jerusalem. The regathering of Jews, the wealth of nations flowing to Israel, and the Millennial Temple are taken as future, physical realities.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — "Arise, shine, for your light has come…"

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** After the thick darkness described in Isaiah 59:9–10, the Redeemer brings rescue. Light has come; God's people must respond. "Darkness is for lying down; light is for rising up." You cannot shine until God's light reaches you, but once it has, there is something wrong if you don't arise and shine. This is no earthly light — it emanates from the glory of the LORD, like the light of Jesus at the Transfiguration (Matt 17:2). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill (older Baptist):** Addressed to the Jewish church, distinct from the Gentiles. "Arise" from a low, dejected state; "shine" — or "be enlightened" — with the light of Christ and the Gospel now come to them. "Thy light is come" means either Christ Himself, the Light of the world, has come spiritually, or the glorious light of the Gospel has come at the time of their conversion, when the blindness is removed and the fullness of the Gentiles brought in (Rom 11:25). [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Zion, the new Jerusalem, has been prostrate in the darkness of Sheol. The word bids her rise to a new life, radiant with the glory of the Lord. Ephesians 5:14 may be an echo (though not a direct quotation) of this verse. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes (Presbyterian/evangelical):** Addressed to the Church, or Zion as the seat of the Church. She has been in affliction; now she is called to arise from the dust. "Shine" means to be encompassed with light and glory — it is prophetic language, not so much a command to impart light as to participate in it. "Thy light is come" refers to the light of the Gospel; the prophet throws himself into future times and sees the Messiah as having already come. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 2 — "For behold, darkness covers the earth… but the LORD will arise upon you"

- **Gill:** The darkness may mean the darkness of ignorance, idolatry, superstition, false doctrine, and false worship covering the nations (Pagan, Mahometan, and Papal darkness) before the light breaks out. Alternatively, it may refer to the distress of the antichristian states when the light breaks forth (Rev 16:10). "The Lord shall arise upon thee" — Christ shall appear in the glory of His person and offices, especially His kingly office. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The darkness that shrouded Zion still spreads over the heathen nations, but they too are to share in the light streaming from the new Jerusalem (cf. Mal 4:2; Ps 84:11). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes:** The rest of the world, except where the Gospel illuminates, is enveloped in deep spiritual night — "gross darkness" (Hebrew *araphel*) denotes a thick cloud or gloomy tempest, a more intense word than ordinary darkness. It describes the pagan world as covered in a cloud of ignorance so dense no light can penetrate it. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 3 — "Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn"

- **Guzik:** When the LORD lifts up His glorious light over Israel, Gentile nations will see it and be attracted. Even kings will be drawn. This will be ultimately fulfilled in the Millennial Kingdom. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill:** "Nations shall walk in thy light" (as in Rev 21:24) — truly regenerated and converted persons. Kings shall be enlightened by Gospel truths and join the church. While only a few of high rank have been called so far, in the latter day "all kings shall serve and worship the Lord" (Ps 72:11). [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Barnes:** This is the main statement the chapter is designed to illustrate — the conversion of the Gentile world. The glory would be so splendid that distant nations and kings would be attracted and come to participate in Gospel blessings. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 4 — "Lift up your eyes and look around… your sons will come from afar"

- **Guzik:** A great theme of regathering. In the Millennial Kingdom, every Jewish person remaining on earth will be gathered into the land of Israel. The present-day regathering is a precious preview of this ultimate regathering. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill:** The "sons" and "daughters" are Jews of the dispersion — children of Abraham, now born again, and therefore Zion's sons. The daughters "nursed at thy side" means being nursed by ministers of the Word with the sincere milk of the Word and the breasts of Gospel ordinances (cf. 1 Thess 2:7). [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Repeated from Isaiah 49:18. The daughters being "nursed at thy side" points to the Eastern custom of carrying young children on the hip of the mother, with their arms clasped round her waist (cf. Isa 66:12). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes:** The "sons" are the dispersed Jewish people driven into exile in distant lands, now regathered. "Nursed at thy side" (Hebrew *aman*) properly means to bear, sustain, or carry a child (Num 11:12), not necessarily nursing. It implies the church's deep solicitude for the young. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 5 — "Then you will look and be radiant… the riches of the sea will be brought to you"

- **Gill:** "Then thou shalt see, and flow together" — there will be a flow of joy like a river when seeing sons and daughters flocking from all parts. The heart shall "fear" — be surprised — and be "enlarged" with love. "The abundance of the sea" means an abundance of converted seafaring men, or the inhabitants of the islands (such as Great Britain and others). "The forces of the Gentiles" means their armies — the soldiery will be converted. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** "Then thou shalt see" — a variant reading gives "thou shalt fear." The heart "shall throb" with awe-stricken joy at the marvellous prosperity, followed by expansion of ecstatic joy. "The abundance of the sea" = the riches of the Western isles, as Tyre and Sidon had been of old (Ezek 27). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes:** "Flow together" (Hebrew *nahar*) may mean to shine or be bright, hence to rejoice. The heart "shall fear" — be ruffled, agitated, deeply excited by the evidence of divine favor. The "abundance of the sea" refers to the wealth of lands beyond the sea being consecrated to the church. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 6 — "Caravans of camels… from Midian and Ephah… from Sheba… bearing gold and frankincense"

- **Guzik:** The nations willingly give their wealth, much as the Egyptians gave riches to Israel at the Exodus (Ex 12:35–36). They do so because they recognize they are giving it to God and because they see God's work in Israel. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill:** Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:4); his posterity inhabited Arabia. This is a prophecy of the conversion of the Arabians. Sheba (also from Abraham by Keturah, Gen 25:3) — the people will bring gold and incense, as the wise men did to Christ. The Sabaeans were famously wealthy in frankincense, myrrh, cinnamon, gold, and silver. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** This verse paints the commerce of the East (v. 5 described the West). Midian and Ephah (Gen 25:4) are noted for camels and riches (Judges 6:5; 8:26). Sheba is famous for gold and incense (Ps 72:10; Strabo xvi.4.19). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes:** The camel is "the ship of the desert," constituting Arabia's wealth. Sheba was probably in Abyssinia (Ethiopia), south of Egypt, known for gold and incense. The picture is that Africa's wealth will be consecrated to the true religion. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 7 — "All the flocks of Kedar… the rams of Nebaioth… I will adorn My glorious house"

- **Gill:** Kedar and Nebaioth were sons of Ishmael (Gen 25:13), inhabiting the country from the Euphrates to the Red Sea — these represent the Turks and Saracens who shall be converted. Their flocks will not be for literal sacrifice, but the best of their substance will serve the interest of Christ. They "come up with acceptance on My altar" through Christ, who is the altar that sanctifies every gift. "I will glorify the house of my glory" — the church, where God dwells and manifests His glory. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Kedar represents the nomad tribes; Nebaioth expanded into the kingdom of the Nabathæan Arabs (Arabia Felix and Arabia Petræa). The primary thought is that the Temple of the new Jerusalem will be supplied with sacrifices from the inexhaustible flocks of these regions. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Barnes:** Kedar (from Ishmael, Gen 25:13) lived in the Arabian desert, rich in flocks. Nebaioth also descended from Ishmael. The idea is that the wealth of these nomadic tribes will be consecrated to God. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 8 — "Who are these who fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters?"

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** A whole sermon on this verse. The Church is filled with three feelings: **(1) Wonder** — at the vast number of converts ("fly as a cloud," not solitary converts but multitudes). Why should we be astonished? Peter saw 3,000 converted under one sermon. **(2) Unity** — "as a cloud" (singular), not "clouds," signifying one united, compact mass. United we are invincible; divided, we are conquered. **(3) Anxiety** — "Who are they?" The Church anxiously desires to be sure the converts are genuine. They are "those that fly" — fleeing from sin, escaping hell, not self-righteous but poor souls who have no rest anywhere and fly with rapid wing to Christ. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-60.html)

- **Gill:** Compared to a "cloud" for their number, for being raised from an earthly to a heavenly state, for being filled with the grace of God (as clouds with water), for unanimity in coming together, and for swiftness in motion to Christ. "As doves to their windows" — doves are clean, amiable, chaste, harmless, meek, humble, weak, and timorous. Dove-houses represent Christ and His church, where converts flee for rest and shelter. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The prophet sees the cloud-like sails of ships bringing back exiles over the Mediterranean and Red Seas, hastening like doves to their dove-cote (cf. Hosea 11:11). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 9 — "Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead…"

- **Gill:** "The isles" — particularly Great Britain, which waited for the Gospel and readily received it early, and where many now wait for the spiritual coming of Christ. "Ships of Tarshish" — Tarshish here means the sea itself (as the Targum renders it, "ships of the sea"), and Gill suggests the ships of Great Britain, "so famous for shipping, and which claims the sovereignty of the seas," will be employed to bring converted Jews and their substance. Just as Israel came out of Egypt with silver and gold, so converted Jews will honour the Lord with their substance. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** "The isles" = far-off maritime regions of the West (as in Isa 49:1). "Ships of Tarshish" = first-class trading ships, whether trading with Spain or in the Indian Ocean (cf. 1 Kings 10:22; 22:48). The mention of silver and gold may point to Ophir as well as Spain. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 10 — "Foreigners will rebuild your walls, and their kings will serve you"

- **Guzik:** The nations willingly build Israel's walls and serve her, not because she deserves it but because they recognize God's glory in her. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill:** "Sons of strangers" = Gentiles who were strangers to God and the covenants. Being converted, they will be useful in building up the Church, strengthening and defending it. "Their kings shall minister unto thee" — though few kings have done so yet (Constantine and some others), when this prophecy is fulfilled it will be general; kings shall be nursing fathers and queens nursing mothers (Isa 49:23). The smiting "in wrath" refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and the blindness on Israel; the mercy refers to their future calling (Rom 11:25). [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The sons of strangers build either as willing proselytes or as those brought into subjection — building the temples or palaces of conquerors was the lot of the conquered (as in Egyptian and Babylonian bondage). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 11 — "Your gates will always stand open…"

- **Ellicott:** Implies (1) a state of peace with no danger of attack, and (2) a constant stream of caravans of pilgrims with offerings entering by night as well as day. St. John transfers the thought to the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev 21:25–26). "That their kings may be brought" — the verb implies they are brought as captives, acknowledging (with or against their will) the sovereignty of Zion. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Gill:** Expresses the peaceable state of the Church — no danger or fear of enemies, none to hurt in all the holy mountain. Also the large numbers of converts streaming in continually. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

---

### v. 12 — "For the nation or kingdom that will not serve you will perish"

- **Guzik:** This is a strong warning — nations that refuse to serve Israel in the Millennial Kingdom will be destroyed. It is the contrast to the Abrahamic blessing. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

---

### v. 13 — "The glory of Lebanon will come to you… to adorn the place of My sanctuary"

- **Guzik:** The riches pouring into Jerusalem in the Millennial Kingdom will be used to build and support the Millennial Temple described in Ezekiel 40–47. There will be priests and sacrifices, but not for atonement — atonement was finished at the cross. The sacrifices are for worship, consecration, and perhaps historical reenactment. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** A revival of the glories of Solomon's days. The cedars of Lebanon and other trees will furnish timber for buildings or be planted in the courts of the Temple. "The place of My feet" is parallel with "sanctuary" — the Temple is called God's footstool (Ps 99:5; 132:7). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 14 — "The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you"

- **Guzik:** Those who previously persecuted Israel and Jerusalem will have a different heart in the Millennial Kingdom. They will recognize Jerusalem as "The City of the LORD." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** The "sons" are named because the persecutors themselves are thought of as no more — or it reflects the law of inherited retribution: the descendants of the old oppressors will prostrate themselves and acknowledge that the restored city is indeed "Zion of the Holy One of Israel." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### vv. 15–16 — "Whereas you have been forsaken and despised… I will make you an everlasting pride… You will drink the milk of nations"

- **Gill:** "Forsaken and hated, so that no one went through you" — the state of the Jewish people during their long dispersion, their land a desolation. But God will make Zion "an eternal excellence, a joy of many generations." The nursing metaphor ("milk of the Gentiles… breast of kings") already appeared in milder form in Isaiah 49:23 — the new Jerusalem shall be supported by the offerings of the Gentiles. "Thou shalt know that I, the LORD, am thy Saviour" — this explains why God does this: not because Israel earned it, but so all will know it is His doing. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm) and [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 17 — "Instead of bronze I will bring you gold… I will appoint peace as your governor"

- **Guzik:** More miraculous than turning bronze to gold is turning magistrates to righteousness. The ultimate fulfillment awaits the Millennial Kingdom, but the principles can begin now in Christian homes and communities. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** The material wealth of Solomon's day (1 Kings 10:21–27) furnishes the picture, but with a striking difference: Solomon's "officers" and "exactors" had been instruments of oppression (1 Kings 12:4), whereas now they will embody righteousness and peace — and therefore prosperity. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 18 — "No longer will violence be heard in your land… you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise"

- **Guzik:** What a transformation — from the violence and bloodshed of Isaiah 59:6–8 to walls called Salvation and gates called Praise. This can begin now: a Christian home can see violence replaced by peace, its walls called Salvation and its doors Praise. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** Freedom from internal misgovernment rather than external invasion. The naming of walls echoes Isaiah 26:1 and likely finds a starting-point in the Eastern practice of giving walls names implying consecration (e.g., the walls of Babylon were named Imgur Bel and Nimetti Belkit). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### vv. 19–20 — "No longer will the sun be your light by day… the LORD will be your everlasting light"

- **Guzik:** This echoes the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21:23, where the LORD Himself is the light. Just as important as having the LORD as your light is having "your God your glory" — glorying in no one or nothing else. "In the old order of creation, life was governed rigidly by night and day… But in the new order of salvation, the ruling principle is the changeless presence of the Lord" (Motyer). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Gill:** This refers to the more perfect state of the Church in the personal reign of Christ — the perfection of light and righteousness. Sun and moon may still shine, but they will not be needed. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/60.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The picture becomes bolder and more transcendent. Sun and moon may still shine, but as in Revelation 21:23 (obviously derived from this), they shall not be needed in the radiance of the greater glory of Jehovah's presence. On earth the sun sets and the moon wanes; in that Divine glory there is no waning and no setting. Mourning belongs to the past (Rev 21:4); everlasting joy to the future. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 21 — "Then all your people will be righteous; they will possess the land forever… the branch of My planting"

- **Guzik:** Written under the shadow of coming defeat and exile, Isaiah points the dispossessed people to a day when "they shall inherit the land forever." This would not be because they were so good, but it would be seen as "the work of My hands, that I may be glorified." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** The city realizes the unfulfilled ideal of Psalms 15 and 24 — evil is blotted out; therefore there is no forfeiture of the inheritance. The "branch" (same word as in Isaiah 11:1) is extended from the ideal representative of the nation (the Messiah) to the whole body of the people. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

---

### v. 22 — "The least of you will become a thousand… I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly"

- **Guzik:** God does not say it will happen soon (though on an eternal scale it may be "soon"), but He will "hasten it" — hurry it along, expedite it — "in its time." When its time has come, He will hasten it, but not before its time. "The promise seems too good to be true… But God is too good not to be true." [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Ellicott:** "A little one" is probably not merely numerical — the Hebrew word refers to a clan or sub-division of a tribe (as in Judges 6:15; 1 Sam 23:23; Micah 5:2). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** "I Jehovah, will hasten it in His time." The neuter refers to everything predicted from v. 1 onwards. Jehovah will fulfil it rapidly when the point of time (*kairos*) which He has fixed for it shall have arrived. As this point of time is known to Him only, the predicted glory remains a matter of faith. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/isaiah-60.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Israel vs. Church.** The biggest difference concerns the identity of "Zion" in the chapter:

- **Dispensational Premillennial (Guzik/Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic):** The prophecy is addressed to ethnic Israel and awaits literal fulfillment in a future Millennial Kingdom. "Replacement theology just doesn't work here, or anywhere." The regathering of Jews to the land, the wealth of nations flowing to Jerusalem, the Millennial Temple, and the nations serving Israel are all taken as future, physical realities. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/)

- **Traditional Amillennial/Postmillennial (Barnes, Gill, Matthew Henry):** The chapter describes the Gospel age — the ingathering of Gentiles into the Christian Church. Barnes says it "refers to the time of the Messiah" and was designed "to foretell the conversion of the pagan world." The Church (Zion) is the focus, not ethnic Israel per se. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-60.html)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Holds a middle position — the prophecy describes "the redeemed Zion — i.e., the new Jerusalem" seen under the forms of the old. It merges the literal and the spiritual, with Revelation 21 as the ultimate fulfillment. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

**The sacrifices of v. 7.** Guzik explicitly says the sacrifices in the Millennial Temple are "not for atonement — because atonement was finished at the cross" but for "worship, consecration, and perhaps historical reenactment." This is a distinctively dispensational way of handling the apparent contradiction with Hebrews. Ellicott treats them more as poetic imagery drawn from the old order. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-60/) and [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-60.html)

**The "milk of nations" and prosperity language (vv. 5, 11, 16–17).** These verses have sometimes been used in prosperity-gospel and Word of Faith teaching to claim that God promises material wealth to believers now. The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes this chapter "has been put through many interpretations… to prove the doctrine that the Church should live by the endowment of the kingdoms of this world." Guzik, by contrast, applies the prosperity to the Millennial Kingdom (future), while also seeing principles for transformation in Christian homes today. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-60.html)

---

## Other Views

**The Expositor's Bible Commentary (mainline Protestant):** Notes that "nothing is said of a Messiah or a King" — Jerusalem is to be a commonwealth, with God Himself as light and glory. "Thus the chapter ends with God and the People, and nothing else." Also observes the "very obvious mingling of the material and the moral" in the chapter. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-60.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/isaiah-60.html)

**Use as Epiphany Lesson:** The chapter is the traditional Lesson for Epiphany in the Christian year, read as describing the ingathering of Gentiles to the Church — a use noted in the Expositor's Bible Commentary.
